sectionTitle: A simple model of the atom, symbols, relative atomic mass, electronic charge and isotopes

specStatements.text: All substances are made of atoms. An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist.
Atoms of each element are represented by a chemical symbol, eg O represents an atom of oxygen, Na represents an atom of sodium.
There are about 100 different elements. Elements are shown in the periodic table.

Compounds are formed from elements by chemical reactions. Chemical reactions always involve the formation of one or more new substances, and often involve a detectable energy change. Compounds contain two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions and can be represented by formulae using the symbols of the atoms from which they were formed. Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions.
Chemical reactions can be represented by word equations or equations using symbols and formulae.
Students will be supplied with a periodic table for the exam and should be able to:
use the names and symbols of the first 20 elements in the periodic table, the elements in Groups 1 and 7, and other elements in this specification
name compounds of these elements from given formulae or symbol equations
write word equations for the reactions in this specification
write formulae and balanced chemical equations for the reactions in this specification.
(HT only) write balanced half equations and ionic equations where appropriate.
A mixture consists of two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined together. The chemical properties of each substance in the mixture are unchanged.

Mixtures can be separated by physical processes such as filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation, fractional distillation and chromatography. These physical processes do not involve chemical reactions and no new substances are made.
Students should be able to:
describe, explain and give examples of the specified processes of separation
suggest suitable separation and purification techniques for mixtures when given appropriate information.
New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.
Before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided.
The discovery of the electron led to the plum pudding model of the atom. The plum pudding model suggested that the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.

The results from the alpha particle scattering experiment led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom was concentrated at the centre (nucleus) and that the nucleus was charged. This nuclear model replaced the plum pudding model.
Niels Bohr adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances. The theoretical calculations of Bohr agreed with experimental observations.

Later experiments led to the idea that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each particle having the same amount of positive charge. The name proton was given to these particles.
The experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence to show the existence of neutrons within the nucleus. This was about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted scientific idea.
Students should be able to describe:
why the new evidence from the scattering experiment led to a change in the atomic model
the difference between the plum pudding model of the atom and the nuclear model of the atom.
Details of experimental work supporting the Bohr model are not required.
Details of Chadwick’s experimental work are not required.
The relative electrical charges of the particles in atoms are:
In an atom, the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons in the nucleus. Atoms have no overall electrical charge.
The number of protons in an atom of an element is its atomic number. All atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons. Atoms of different elements have different numbers of protons.
Atoms are very small, having a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m).
The radius of a nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of that of the atom (about 1 x 10⁻¹⁴ m).
Almost all of the mass of an atom is in the nucleus.
The relative masses of protons, neutrons and electrons are:
The sum of the protons and neutrons in an atom is its mass number.
Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these atoms are called isotopes of that element.
Atoms can be represented as shown in this example:
Students should be able to calculate the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom or ion, given its atomic number and mass number.
Students should be able to relate size and scale of atoms to objects in the physical world.
The relative atomic mass of an element is an average value that takes account of the abundance of the isotopes of the element.

The electrons in an atom occupy the lowest available energy levels (innermost available shells). The electronic structure of an atom can be represented by numbers or by a diagram. For example, the electronic structure of sodium is 2,8,1 or
showing two electrons in the lowest energy level, eight in the second energy level and one in the third energy level.
Students may answer questions in terms of either energy levels or shells.

scopeNotes.statement: Students will be supplied with a periodic table for the exam and should be able to:
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Nothing here asks a student to recall periodic table data from memory. Where a question needs an atomic number, a mass number or the composition of an atom, the stem supplies it (eg the symbol ⁴⁰₁₈Ar or the number of electrons). Only the names and symbols listed in the specification itself – the first 20 elements, Groups 1 and 7, and elements named elsewhere in the specification – are tested directly.

scopeNotes.statement: Details of experimental work supporting the Bohr model are not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The Bohr items ask only what Bohr suggested (electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances) and that his theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations. No spectral line evidence, no apparatus and no data from that work appear in any concept, misconception or question.

scopeNotes.statement: Details of Chadwick’s experimental work are not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Chadwick appears only as the scientist whose experimental work provided evidence for neutrons in the nucleus, about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted idea. No apparatus, particles used, or measurements from his experiments are described or examined.

scopeNotes.statement: Students may answer questions in terms of either energy levels or shells.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every concept, misconception and question that deals with electronic structure names both terms, and no item is marked wrong for using one rather than the other. Stems are written as 'energy levels (shells)' so neither wording is privileged.

concepts.definition: The smallest part of an element that can exist. All substances are made of atoms.
A substance made of only one type of atom. There are about 100 different elements, and they are shown in the periodic table.

The letter or letters used to represent an atom of an element, eg O represents an atom of oxygen and Na represents an atom of sodium. The first letter is a capital and any second letter is lower case.
The table in which the elements are shown. It is supplied to students in the exam, so element symbols and data are read from it rather than recalled.

A substance containing two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions. It can be represented by a formula using the symbols of the atoms from which it was formed, and can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions.
A change that always involves the formation of one or more new substances, and often involves a detectable energy change. Compounds are formed from elements by chemical reactions.
A representation of a compound using the symbols of the atoms from which it was formed, with numbers showing how many of each atom, eg H₂O, CaCO₃, Mg(NO₃)₂.
A representation of a chemical reaction using the names of the substances, with reactants on the left, an arrow, and products on the right, eg zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen.

A representation of a reaction using symbols and formulae in which there is the same number of atoms of each element on both sides of the arrow, eg 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. It is balanced by placing numbers in front of formulae, never by changing a formula.
An equation showing the electrons lost or gained by one species, eg Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na at the cathode and 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ at the anode. Both atoms and charges must balance.
An equation showing only the species that take part in the reaction, with ions that are unchanged left out, eg Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu.
Two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined together. The chemical properties of each substance in the mixture are unchanged.
A physical process that separates an insoluble solid from a liquid: the liquid passes through the filter paper and the solid stays behind as a residue.
A physical process that separates a soluble solid from its solution: the solvent is evaporated, leaving the solid behind as crystals.
A physical process that separates a solvent from a solution: the solvent evaporates, then condenses back to a liquid and is collected, leaving the solute behind.
A physical process that separates two or more miscible liquids using the differences in their boiling points, with the fractionating column separating liquids whose boiling points are close.
A physical process that separates substances in a mixture using their different solubilities in the solvent: the more soluble a substance is, the further it is carried up the paper.

A way of separating a mixture that does not involve a chemical reaction, so no new substances are made. Filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation, fractional distillation and chromatography are all physical processes.
An idea used to explain observations. New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.
The model held before the discovery of the electron, in which atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided.
The model that followed the discovery of the electron. It suggested that the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
The experiment whose results led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom was concentrated at the centre (nucleus) and that the nucleus was charged.
The model in which the mass of the atom is concentrated in a small charged nucleus at the centre. It replaced the plum pudding model.
Niels Bohr's adaptation of the nuclear model, suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances. His theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations.
The name given to the smaller particles into which the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided, each particle having the same amount of positive charge.
The particle within the nucleus whose existence was shown by the experimental work of James Chadwick, about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted scientific idea.
The charge on each particle compared with the others: proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1.
An atom has no overall electrical charge because the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons in the nucleus.
The number of protons in an atom of an element. All atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons, and atoms of different elements have different numbers of protons.
Atoms are very small, having a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m).
Less than 1/10 000 of the radius of the atom (about 1 x 10⁻¹⁴ m).

concepts.term: Distribution of mass in an atom
concepts.definition: Almost all of the mass of an atom is in the nucleus, because that is where the protons and neutrons are.
Proton 1, neutron 1, electron very small.
The sum of the protons and neutrons in an atom.
Atoms of the same element that have different numbers of neutrons, and therefore the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
The way an atom is represented, with the mass number written above the atomic number and both written before the chemical symbol, eg ²³₁₁Na.
An atom that has an overall electrical charge because it has lost or gained electrons. Its number of protons is unchanged, so a 2+ ion has two fewer electrons than protons.
An average value for an element that takes account of the abundance of the isotopes of the element.

A region around the nucleus that electrons occupy. In sodium, 2,8,1 shows two electrons in the lowest energy level, eight in the second and one in the third. Answers may use either 'energy level' or 'shell'.
The arrangement of the electrons in an atom, represented by numbers or by a diagram. Electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels (innermost available shells) first.

misconceptions.question: What is an atom the smallest part of?
misconceptions.correct: An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist.
misconceptions.misconception: An atom is the smallest thing there is – nothing can be smaller than an atom.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'atom' is often introduced as 'the smallest particle', and the qualifier 'of an element' is dropped in everyday speech.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is precise: an atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist. Atoms themselves contain smaller particles – protons, neutrons and electrons – and the whole story of the atomic model is the story of finding them.

misconceptions.question: Can a single atom be made of two different elements?
misconceptions.correct: No. An atom is a particle of one element only; a particle containing two or more different elements is a particle of a compound.
misconceptions.misconception: An atom of water is H₂O, so one atom can contain hydrogen and oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Formulae such as H₂O are read as the name of one 'particle', and the words atom, molecule and compound are used loosely.
misconceptions.correction: H₂O shows a compound formed from the elements hydrogen and oxygen; it contains three atoms, two of hydrogen and one of oxygen. Each atom belongs to one element only.

misconceptions.question: Why is the symbol for sodium Na and not S?
misconceptions.correct: Symbols are not always the first letters of the English name; sodium is Na and potassium is K.
misconceptions.misconception: Every symbol is just the first letter or two of the element's English name, so sodium must be S or So.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most of the symbols met first (C, O, H, Mg, Ca) do follow the English name, so the pattern is over-generalised.
misconceptions.correction: Some symbols come from older names (natrium, kalium, ferrum). The periodic table is supplied in the exam, so symbols such as Na, K, Fe and Pb should be read from it rather than guessed.

misconceptions.question: Does it matter whether a symbol is written CO or Co?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Co is the symbol for one element, cobalt; CO is a formula for a compound of carbon and oxygen.
misconceptions.misconception: Capital and small letters in chemistry are just handwriting – CO and Co mean the same thing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In most writing capitalisation carries no meaning, so students treat chemical symbols the same way.
misconceptions.correction: In a symbol the first letter is always a capital and any second letter is always lower case. Two capitals means two different elements, so CO is carbon joined to oxygen while Co is a single element.

misconceptions.question: Are compounds shown in the periodic table?
misconceptions.correct: No. The periodic table shows the elements only – about 100 of them.
misconceptions.misconception: The periodic table is a list of all the substances there are, so compounds like water and salt must be somewhere on it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The table is presented as 'the chemistry table', and students do not separate 'substance' from 'element'.
misconceptions.correction: There are about 100 different elements and they are shown in the periodic table. The millions of other substances are compounds and mixtures made from those elements, and none of them appears in the table.

misconceptions.question: Can a compound be separated by filtering or evaporating?
misconceptions.correct: No. Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions.
misconceptions.misconception: Water is hydrogen and oxygen put together, so you should be able to separate it the way you separate any other mixture.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mixtures and compounds are both 'made of more than one thing', so the same separation methods are assumed to work on both.
misconceptions.correction: In a compound the elements are chemically combined in fixed proportions, and only a chemical reaction can break those combinations. Physical processes separate mixtures only.

misconceptions.question: Is melting or dissolving a chemical reaction?
misconceptions.correct: No. A chemical reaction always involves the formation of one or more new substances.
misconceptions.misconception: Something changed and it may have got hotter or colder, so a reaction must have happened.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The specification says reactions often involve a detectable energy change, and students turn that into a test: energy change means reaction.
misconceptions.correction: The energy change is a common feature of reactions, not the definition. The test is whether one or more new substances have been formed. Melting ice and dissolving salt make no new substance.

misconceptions.question: How do you balance Mg + O₂ → MgO?
misconceptions.correct: Put numbers in front of the formulae: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
misconceptions.misconception: Change the little number inside the formula until the atoms match, so write MgO₂.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balancing is seen as a numbers puzzle rather than as a statement about substances, so any number that makes the count work looks acceptable.
misconceptions.correction: The small numbers inside a formula say which substance it is. Changing MgO to MgO₂ changes the product to a different compound. Only the large numbers in front of formulae may be changed.

misconceptions.question: Does a word equation have to be balanced?
misconceptions.correct: No. Word equations use names only and carry no numbers to balance.
misconceptions.misconception: Every equation has to balance, so a word equation needs numbers in front of the names too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balancing is drilled with symbol equations and the rule is then applied to every equation a student meets.
misconceptions.correction: Balancing counts atoms, and names do not show atoms. A word equation simply lists reactants, an arrow, and products. Numbers and formulae belong in the symbol equation.

misconceptions.question: In a half equation, which side do the electrons go on?
misconceptions.correct: Electrons go on the left when they are gained (Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na) and on the right when they are lost (2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻).
misconceptions.misconception: Electrons always go on the same side of a half equation, so I can write it one way every time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Half equations are learned as a shape to copy rather than as a description of electrons moving, so the direction is not checked.
misconceptions.correction: Decide first whether the species gains or loses electrons. A positive ion becoming a neutral atom must gain electrons, so they appear with the reactants; a negative ion becoming a neutral element must lose them, so they appear with the products. Charges must balance on both sides.

misconceptions.question: Should the sulfate ions appear in the ionic equation for zinc and copper sulfate?
misconceptions.correct: No. Ions that are unchanged are left out, giving Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu.
misconceptions.misconception: An ionic equation is just the ordinary equation written with the ions in, so everything present has to be shown.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are taught to write out all the ions as a first step and then stop, without cancelling the ions that are the same on both sides.
misconceptions.correction: An ionic equation shows only the species that change. The sulfate ions are present before and after, unchanged, so they are cancelled from both sides.

misconceptions.question: Do the substances in a mixture keep their own properties?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The chemical properties of each substance in a mixture are unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: Once two substances are mixed they behave as one new substance with new properties.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mixing looks like a change – the appearance is different – so students infer that the substances themselves have changed.
misconceptions.correction: In a mixture the substances are not chemically combined, so each one keeps its own chemical properties. Iron in a mixture with sulfur is still attracted to a magnet; iron in the compound iron sulfide is not.

misconceptions.question: Is separating a mixture a chemical reaction?
misconceptions.correct: No. Filtration, crystallisation, distillation and chromatography are physical processes and no new substances are made.
misconceptions.misconception: Distilling or filtering changes the substance, so a chemical reaction must be taking place.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Heating is involved in distillation and crystallisation, and heating is associated with reactions.
misconceptions.correction: These processes only move substances apart using differences in their physical properties. The substances that come out are the same substances that went in.

misconceptions.question: Can filtration separate salt from salt solution?
misconceptions.correct: No. Filtration only removes an insoluble solid; a dissolved solid passes through the filter paper.
misconceptions.misconception: The filter paper has tiny holes, so it should trap the salt and let the water through.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Filtration is remembered as 'getting a solid out of a liquid', and dissolved salt is still thought of as a solid sitting in the water.
misconceptions.correction: A dissolved solid is broken up among the water particles and passes straight through the paper. To recover a dissolved solid, crystallise the solution instead.

misconceptions.question: How do you collect the water from a copper sulfate solution?
misconceptions.correct: By simple distillation: the water evaporates, condenses and is collected.
misconceptions.misconception: Crystallise it – that separates the solution, so the water will be collected too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Crystallisation and distillation are both taught as 'ways of separating a solution', so students pick either without asking which part they want to keep.
misconceptions.correction: Crystallisation keeps the solute and loses the solvent to the air. If the solvent is the part you want, it must be condensed and collected, which is simple distillation.

misconceptions.question: When is fractional distillation needed rather than simple distillation?
misconceptions.correct: When separating liquids that are mixed together and have boiling points close to each other.
misconceptions.misconception: Fractional distillation is the better method, so it should be used for any solution, including salt water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'fractional' sounds more advanced, so it is assumed to be the stronger version of the same method.
misconceptions.correction: Simple distillation is enough when only one component evaporates, as with a solution of a solid. A fractionating column is needed when two or more liquids both evaporate and their boiling points are close.

misconceptions.question: In chromatography, which substance travels furthest up the paper?
misconceptions.correct: The most soluble substance in the solvent used travels furthest.
misconceptions.misconception: The lightest or least soluble substance travels furthest because nothing holds it back.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture the solvent 'pushing' particles along and reason about weight, rather than about how well each substance dissolves.
misconceptions.correction: The solvent carries a substance up the paper only while that substance is dissolved in it. The more soluble a substance is, the more of the time it travels and the further up the paper it ends up.

misconceptions.question: Can a scientific model change after it has been accepted?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. New experimental evidence may lead to a model being changed or replaced.
misconceptions.misconception: Once scientists accept a model it has been proved, so it is fixed and cannot be replaced.
misconceptions.whyItArises: School science is met as settled fact, so models look like final answers rather than the current best explanation.
misconceptions.correction: The atomic model has been changed repeatedly: indivisible spheres, then plum pudding, then the nuclear model, then Bohr's orbits. Each change came from new experimental evidence that the old model could not explain.

misconceptions.question: Where are the electrons in the plum pudding model?
misconceptions.correct: Embedded in a ball of positive charge that fills the whole atom.
misconceptions.misconception: The plum pudding model has electrons going round the outside of a positive centre.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every picture of an atom students have seen shows electrons orbiting, so that image is attached to the wrong model.
misconceptions.correction: Orbiting electrons and a central nucleus belong to the nuclear and Bohr models. In the plum pudding model there is no nucleus and no orbit – the positive charge is spread through the whole atom with electrons stuck in it.

misconceptions.question: What happened to most of the alpha particles in the scattering experiment?
misconceptions.correct: Most passed straight through the foil without being deflected.
misconceptions.misconception: Most of the alpha particles bounced back, which is how they knew the nucleus was there.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The surprising result – a few particles coming straight back – is the one that gets remembered, so it is assumed to be the common one.
misconceptions.correction: Only a small number were deflected and very few came back. That most passed straight through showed the atom is mostly empty space; that a few were repelled strongly showed the mass and charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.

misconceptions.question: What conclusion came from the alpha particle scattering experiment?
misconceptions.correct: That the mass of an atom is concentrated at the centre in a charged nucleus.
misconceptions.misconception: The scattering experiment showed that electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed shells.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The scattering experiment and Bohr's model are taught close together, so their conclusions merge.
misconceptions.correction: The scattering results established the nucleus itself. Electrons at specific distances were Bohr's later suggestion, supported by his theoretical calculations agreeing with observations.

misconceptions.question: What did Bohr contribute?
misconceptions.correct: He adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances.
misconceptions.misconception: Bohr was the one who discovered the nucleus and showed the atom's mass is at its centre.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Bohr's name is attached to the familiar shell diagram, which students treat as the whole model including the nucleus.
misconceptions.correction: The nucleus came from the alpha particle scattering results. Bohr started from that nuclear model and added the idea of specific orbit distances, which his calculations then supported.

misconceptions.question: What did James Chadwick's work provide evidence for?
misconceptions.correct: The existence of neutrons within the nucleus.
misconceptions.misconception: Chadwick discovered the proton, or the nucleus itself.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The three sub-atomic particles are learned as one list, so the names of the scientists attached to them get swapped.
misconceptions.correction: The electron came first, then the nucleus from scattering, then protons as the subdivided positive charge. Chadwick's evidence for neutrons came about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted idea.

misconceptions.question: Were protons identified at the same time as the nucleus?
misconceptions.correct: No. The nucleus came first; later experiments showed its positive charge could be subdivided into protons.
misconceptions.misconception: The scattering experiment found the nucleus, so it found the protons in it at the same time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Positive nucleus' and 'protons' are used interchangeably in later work, hiding the fact that they were separate discoveries.
misconceptions.correction: The scattering results showed only that the centre was massive and charged. It was later experiments that showed the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each with the same amount of positive charge, which were named protons.

misconceptions.question: What is the relative charge and relative mass of a neutron?
misconceptions.correct: Its relative charge is 0 and its relative mass is 1.
misconceptions.misconception: A neutron has no charge, so it has no mass either – it is like nothing at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Neutral' and 'nothing' sound alike, and the neutron is the particle least often drawn as doing anything.
misconceptions.correction: Charge and mass are separate properties. The neutron has zero relative charge but a relative mass of 1, the same as the proton, so it contributes just as much to the mass number.

misconceptions.question: How does the mass of an electron compare with that of a proton?
misconceptions.correct: The relative mass of an electron is very small compared with 1 for a proton.
misconceptions.misconception: Protons, neutrons and electrons all have a relative mass of about 1.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The three particles are listed together in one table, so students assume all three rows carry similar values.
misconceptions.correction: Protons and neutrons each have a relative mass of 1; the electron's relative mass is very small. This is why almost all of the mass of an atom is in the nucleus.

misconceptions.question: Why does an atom have no overall charge?
misconceptions.correct: Because the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons.
misconceptions.misconception: An atom is neutral because it has the same number of protons and neutrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Neutrons are 'the neutral ones', so they are assumed to be the reason the atom is neutral.
misconceptions.correction: Neutrons have no charge, so they cannot cancel anything. Neutrality comes from equal numbers of the two charged particles: each +1 proton is matched by a −1 electron.

misconceptions.question: What is the atomic number of an element?
misconceptions.correct: The number of protons in an atom of the element.
misconceptions.misconception: The atomic number is the total number of particles in the nucleus.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Atomic number' and 'mass number' are both numbers about the nucleus, and the words give no clue which is which.
misconceptions.correction: The atomic number counts protons only, and it is what identifies the element. The number of protons and neutrons added together is the mass number.

misconceptions.question: How big is a nucleus compared with the whole atom?
misconceptions.correct: Its radius is less than 1/10 000 of the radius of the atom.
misconceptions.misconception: The nucleus is about a tenth of the size of the atom – like the picture in the textbook.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams have to draw the nucleus large enough to see, so the drawn proportions are taken as real.
misconceptions.correction: An atom has a radius of about 1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m and a nucleus about 1 x 10⁻¹⁴ m: ten thousand times smaller. A true-to-scale diagram of an atom the size of a room would need a nucleus smaller than a grain of sand.

misconceptions.question: What does the mass number count?
misconceptions.correct: The sum of the protons and neutrons in an atom.
misconceptions.misconception: The mass number is the total of the protons, the neutrons and the electrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mass number is read as 'the number of everything in the atom', and electrons are particles too.
misconceptions.correction: Electrons have a very small relative mass, so they are not counted. The mass number is protons + neutrons only.

misconceptions.question: What is different about the atoms in a pair of isotopes?
misconceptions.correct: They have different numbers of neutrons and so different mass numbers.
misconceptions.misconception: Isotopes are atoms of an element with different numbers of protons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Isotopes are introduced as 'atoms of the same element that are different', and protons are the number students reach for first.
misconceptions.correction: Changing the number of protons changes the element itself. Isotopes are atoms of the same element, so the number of protons is fixed and only the number of neutrons differs.

misconceptions.question: Are isotopes atoms with different numbers of electrons?
misconceptions.correct: No. Isotopes differ in neutrons; atoms with different numbers of electrons from protons are ions.
misconceptions.misconception: Isotopes have gained or lost electrons, which is what makes them different.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Isotope' and 'ion' are both words for an atom that is not the standard one, and they are met in the same few lessons.
misconceptions.correction: An isotope is a neutral atom of the element with a different number of neutrons. An ion has lost or gained electrons and so carries an overall charge.

misconceptions.question: In ²³₁₁Na, which number is the mass number?
misconceptions.correct: 23, the number written above; 11 below it is the atomic number.
misconceptions.misconception: The number on top is the atomic number because atomic number is mentioned first in the notes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: There is no clue in the notation itself, so students rely on the order the two terms were taught in.
misconceptions.correction: The larger number is always the mass number and it is written above; the atomic number is written below. Checking helps: the mass number cannot be smaller than the atomic number.

misconceptions.question: How does an atom become a 2+ ion?
misconceptions.correct: It loses two electrons; the number of protons does not change.
misconceptions.misconception: A 2+ charge means the atom has gained two extra protons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Charge is linked to protons because protons are the positive particles, so a positive charge suggests more of them.
misconceptions.correction: The number of protons fixes which element the particle is and never changes in chemical reactions. A 2+ ion has two fewer electrons than protons, so Mg²⁺ still has 12 protons but only 10 electrons.

misconceptions.question: What does a relative atomic mass of 35.5 for chlorine mean?
misconceptions.correct: It is an average value taking account of the abundance of chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.
misconceptions.misconception: It is the mass of the most common chlorine isotope, so every chlorine atom weighs 35.5.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Relative atomic mass is read off the periodic table as a property of one atom, so it is applied to every atom of the element.
misconceptions.correction: No single atom has a mass number of 35.5; mass numbers are whole numbers. The value is an average across the isotopes, weighted by how abundant each one is.

misconceptions.question: Is relative atomic mass just the average of the isotopes' mass numbers?
misconceptions.correct: No. It takes account of the abundance of each isotope, not just their mass numbers.
misconceptions.misconception: Chlorine has isotopes 35 and 37, so its relative atomic mass is (35 + 37) ÷ 2 = 36.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Average' is understood only as 'add them up and divide', which ignores how much of each isotope there is.
misconceptions.correction: A plain average would only be right if the isotopes were equally abundant. Chlorine-35 is much more common than chlorine-37, which pulls the average down to 35.5.

misconceptions.question: Which energy level do electrons fill first?
misconceptions.correct: The lowest available energy level (the innermost available shell).
misconceptions.misconception: Electrons go into the outer shell first, or spread themselves evenly between the shells.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams are often drawn from the outside in, and the outer shell is the one talked about most because it controls bonding.
misconceptions.correction: Electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels first, so the innermost shell is filled before the next one is started. Sodium is 2,8,1 and never 1,8,2.

misconceptions.question: What is the electronic structure of potassium, which has 19 electrons?
misconceptions.misconception: 2,8,9, because the third energy level can hold more than eight electrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students hear that the third level can eventually hold more than eight and apply that to the elements met at GCSE.
misconceptions.correction: For the first 20 elements the third energy level takes eight electrons and then the fourth begins. Potassium is 2,8,8,1 and calcium is 2,8,8,2.

misconceptions.question: Are 'nitride', 'nitrite' and 'nitrate' the same thing?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are different compounds, and the ending must be right.
misconceptions.misconception: The ending of the name does not matter much – nitride and nitrate both mean nitrogen is in there.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The endings sound almost identical and are barely audible in speech, so they are treated as spelling variants.
misconceptions.correction: An -ide ending usually means just two elements, as in magnesium nitride. An -ate ending means oxygen is also present, as in magnesium nitrate, Mg(NO₃)₂. Naming a compound from its formula depends on reading the ending correctly.

misconceptions.question: Do the numbers in a formula appear in the compound's name?
misconceptions.correct: No. Mg(NO₃)₂ is magnesium nitrate, not magnesium dinitrate.
misconceptions.misconception: There is a 2 in the formula, so the name needs a prefix such as di- to show it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Prefixes are met in names such as carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide, so students generalise the rule to every formula.
misconceptions.correction: For the compounds named in this specification the ratio is fixed by the charges on the ions and is not written into the name. Mg(NO₃)₂ is simply magnesium nitrate.

misconceptions.question: Which element has the symbol Na?
misconceptions.correct: Sodium. Na is a two-letter symbol and both letters belong to it.
misconceptions.misconception: Na starts with N, so it must be nitrogen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Symbols are scanned quickly and only the capital letter registers, especially in a formula such as NaCl.
misconceptions.correction: A symbol is one capital letter, sometimes followed by one lower-case letter. N is nitrogen; Na is sodium. Reading only the capital would also turn Ca into carbon and Cl into carbon.

misconceptions.question: Which charge fills the ball in the plum pudding model?
misconceptions.correct: Positive. The atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
misconceptions.misconception: The pudding is a negative ball with positive bits stuck in it, like currants.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The name is remembered but not which part is which, and the electron is the particle students recall best, so it becomes the 'ball'.
misconceptions.correction: The electrons are the 'plums'; the surrounding 'pudding' is positive. The model was built to explain how negative electrons sit inside an atom that is neutral overall.

misconceptions.question: What is 0.1 nm written in metres?
misconceptions.correct: 1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m.
misconceptions.misconception: 0.1 nm must be 1 x 10⁻⁹ m, or about 0.1 mm – the prefixes are all much the same.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The prefixes milli-, micro- and nano- are learned as 'small' without the powers of ten attached to them, so conversions are guessed.
misconceptions.correction: 1 nm is 1 x 10⁻⁹ m, so 0.1 nm is one tenth of that: 1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m. That is the radius of a typical atom, a hundred million times smaller than a millimetre.

mcqs.stem: Which of these best describes an atom?

options.text: The smallest part of an element that can exist
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition: an atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist.

options.text: The smallest particle of matter that can ever exist
options.rationale: Students who learn 'atom = smallest particle' drop the words 'of an element'; atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons.

options.text: The smallest part of a compound that can ever exist
options.rationale: Confuses the atom with the smallest particle of a compound; a compound is formed from atoms of two or more elements.

options.text: Any particle made of two or more atoms joined together
options.rationale: Describes a particle of a compound, chosen by students who read a formula such as H₂O as 'one atom'.

mcqs.stem: Which is the chemical symbol for an atom of sodium?

options.text: S
options.rationale: Chosen by students who expect the symbol to be the first letter of the English name; S is sulfur.

options.text: Na
options.rationale: Na is the symbol for sodium, taken from its older name natrium.

options.text: N
options.rationale: N is nitrogen; this is the capital letter of Na read on its own.

options.text: NA
options.rationale: Two capitals would mean two elements; the second letter of a symbol is always lower case.

mcqs.stem: Why do CO and Co mean different things?

options.text: They are the same; capitals are only used for neatness
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat capitalisation as handwriting rather than as part of the symbol.

options.text: Co shows a compound; CO shows one element's atom
options.rationale: The right idea reversed, by students who know case matters but not which way round.

options.text: Co is one element, cobalt; CO is carbon joined to oxygen
options.rationale: A capital followed by a lower-case letter is one element's symbol; two capitals are two different elements.

options.text: Co is an atom of cobalt; CO is an atom of a new element
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think combining two elements produces a single atom of something new.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about elements and the periodic table is correct?

options.text: Elements and compounds are both shown in the periodic table
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read the table as a list of every substance rather than of elements.

options.text: About 100 substances exist in total, so they are all elements
options.rationale: Confuses the number of elements with the number of substances; compounds run to millions.

options.text: Elements appear in the periodic table only if found naturally
options.rationale: The table shows about 100 elements whether or not they occur naturally.

options.text: About 100 elements exist and they are shown in the table
options.rationale: There are about 100 different elements and the periodic table shows them.

mcqs.stem: Which of these describes a compound?

options.text: Two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition of a compound.

options.text: Two or more elements mixed together in any proportions you like
options.rationale: Describes a mixture; students who treat compounds and mixtures as the same choose it.

options.text: Two or more substances that keep their own chemical properties
options.rationale: This is the mixture definition; in a compound the elements are chemically combined.

options.text: Two or more atoms of the same single element chemically joined
options.rationale: A substance made of only one type of atom is an element, not a compound.

mcqs.stem: Which of these changes is a chemical reaction?

options.text: Ice melting in a warm room to form liquid water
options.rationale: Energy is taken in, but no new substance forms; the water is the same substance.

options.text: Magnesium burning in air to form magnesium oxide
options.rationale: A new substance, magnesium oxide, is formed, with a detectable energy change.

options.text: Salt dissolving in water to make a salt solution
options.rationale: There is a small energy change, but the salt is unchanged and can be recovered.

options.text: Water evaporating from a puddle to form vapour
options.rationale: A change of state only; the substance formed is still water.

mcqs.stem: Sodium chloride is a compound of sodium and chlorine. How can it be separated into those elements?

options.text: By filtering it, because the two elements are only mixed together
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat a compound as a mixture of its elements.

options.text: By distilling it, since the elements have different boiling points
options.rationale: Distillation is a physical process; it separates mixtures, not chemically combined elements.

options.text: By a chemical reaction, because compounds need chemical change
options.rationale: Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions.

options.text: By dissolving it in water, which frees up the sodium and chlorine
options.rationale: Dissolving separates the ions in solution but does not produce the elements sodium and chlorine.

mcqs.stem: Zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid to make zinc chloride and hydrogen. Which is the correct word equation?

options.text: zinc chloride + hydrogen → zinc + hydrochloric acid
options.rationale: The reactants and products have been swapped, so the arrow points the wrong way.

options.text: zinc + hydrochloric acid = zinc chloride and hydrogen
options.rationale: Uses an equals sign and 'and'; an equation needs an arrow separating reactants from products.

options.text: 2 zinc + 2 hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think every equation must carry balancing numbers, including word equations.

options.text: zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen
options.rationale: Reactants on the left, an arrow, products on the right, all written as names.

mcqs.stem: Which equation for burning magnesium in oxygen is balanced?

options.text: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
options.rationale: Two Mg and two O on each side, and each formula is correct.

options.text: Mg + O₂ → MgO₂
options.rationale: Balanced by changing the formula, which turns the product into a different compound.

options.text: Mg + O₂ → MgO
options.rationale: Formulae are correct but the oxygen atoms do not balance: two on the left, one on the right.

options.text: 2Mg + O₂ → MgO
options.rationale: The magnesium atoms now do not balance; the number was placed on only one side.

mcqs.stem: Which numbers balance the equation ___H₂ + O₂ → ___H₂O?

options.text: 1 and 1
options.rationale: Leaves two oxygen atoms on the left and only one on the right.

options.text: 2 and 2
options.rationale: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O gives four H and two O on each side.

options.text: 1 and 2
options.rationale: Doubles the water without doubling the hydrogen, so hydrogen no longer balances.

options.text: 2 and 1
options.rationale: Doubles the hydrogen molecules but not the water, leaving hydrogen unbalanced.

mcqs.stem: What is the name of the compound with the formula Mg(NO₃)₂?

options.text: magnesium nitride
options.rationale: An -ide ending means only two elements are present; magnesium nitride is Mg₃N₂.

options.text: magnesium nitrite
options.rationale: Nitrite is NO₂⁻; the formula here shows three oxygen atoms, so it is nitrate.

options.text: magnesium nitrate
options.rationale: The NO₃⁻ ion is nitrate, so the compound is magnesium nitrate.

options.text: magnesium dinitrate
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the 2 in the formula must appear as a prefix in the name.

mcqs.stem: In the equation 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, what is the name of the product?

options.text: sodium chlorate
options.rationale: An -ate ending would mean oxygen is present as well; there is no oxygen here.

options.text: sodium chlorine
options.rationale: The second element in a compound of two elements takes an -ide ending, not its own name.

options.text: disodium chloride
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read the 2 in 2NaCl as part of the compound's name.

options.text: sodium chloride
options.rationale: NaCl is the compound of sodium and chlorine, named sodium chloride.

mcqs.stem: Which element has the symbol P?

options.text: phosphorus
options.rationale: P is phosphorus, one of the first 20 elements.

options.text: potassium
options.rationale: Chosen because potassium begins with P in English; its symbol is actually K.

options.text: platinum
options.rationale: Another element whose English name begins with P; its symbol is Pt.

options.text: lead
options.rationale: Lead's symbol is Pb; only the capital letter has been read.

mcqs.stem: Sodium ions gain electrons at the cathode to form sodium atoms. Which half equation is correct?

options.text: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻
options.rationale: This shows an electron being lost; it is the reverse of what happens at the cathode.

options.text: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na
options.rationale: One electron is gained by each Na⁺ ion; atoms and charges balance.

options.text: Na⁺ → Na + e⁻
options.rationale: Electrons are on the wrong side, so the charge does not balance.

options.text: 2Na⁺ + e⁻ → 2Na
options.rationale: Two ions would need two electrons; as written neither charge nor electrons balance.

mcqs.stem: Chloride ions lose electrons at the anode to form chlorine gas. Which half equation is correct?

options.text: Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻
options.rationale: The reverse process, showing electrons gained rather than lost.

options.text: 2Cl⁻ + 2e⁻ → Cl₂
options.rationale: Electrons placed on the left, so the charges do not balance.

options.text: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
options.rationale: Two chloride ions lose one electron each; atoms and charges balance.

options.text: Cl⁻ → Cl + e⁻
options.rationale: Chlorine gas is Cl₂, so single atoms should not be shown as the product.

mcqs.stem: Zinc displaces copper from copper sulfate solution. Which is the correct ionic equation?

options.text: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu
options.rationale: This is the full equation; the unchanged sulfate ions should be cancelled from an ionic equation.

options.text: Zn²⁺ + Cu → Zn + Cu²⁺
options.rationale: The electron transfer is the wrong way round: zinc loses electrons, copper gains them.

options.text: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu²⁺
options.rationale: Copper is left charged, so the charges do not balance across the equation.

options.text: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu
options.rationale: Only the species that change are shown; the sulfate ions are unchanged and are left out.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes a mixture?

options.text: Substances not chemically combined, each keeping its properties
options.rationale: A mixture is two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined; properties are unchanged.

options.text: Substances that lose their own properties once they are mixed
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think mixing changes the substances themselves.

options.text: Elements chemically combined together in fixed proportions
options.rationale: This is the definition of a compound, not a mixture.

options.text: Substances that can only be separated by a chemical reaction
options.rationale: Mixtures are separated by physical processes; only compounds need chemical reactions.

mcqs.stem: Air contains nitrogen, oxygen and other gases. Why is air a mixture?

options.text: Its gases react together and so lose their own properties
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think substances change when they are mixed.

options.text: Its gases are not chemically combined and keep their properties
options.rationale: The gases are simply mixed, and each still behaves as it always does.

options.text: Its gases are held in fixed proportions by chemical bonding
options.rationale: Fixed proportions and chemical combination describe a compound, not air.

options.text: It can only be separated into its gases by chemical reactions
options.rationale: Air is separated by fractional distillation, a physical process.

mcqs.stem: How would you obtain pure water from copper sulfate solution?

options.text: Filtration, since the filter paper holds back the copper sulfate
options.rationale: Dissolved copper sulfate passes straight through filter paper.

options.text: Crystallisation, since the water is all left behind in the dish
options.rationale: Crystallisation keeps the solute and loses the water to the air.

options.text: Simple distillation, then collect the condensed water vapour
options.rationale: The water evaporates and is condensed and collected; the copper sulfate stays behind.

options.text: Chromatography, since the water travels furthest up the paper
options.rationale: Chromatography separates dissolved substances on paper; it does not collect a pure solvent.

mcqs.stem: Salt is dissolved in water. How is the solid salt recovered?

options.text: Filtration: pour it through filter paper to trap the salt
options.rationale: Dissolved salt passes through the paper with the water.

options.text: Fractional distillation: separate the salt from the water
options.rationale: A fractionating column separates liquids of similar boiling point, not a dissolved solid.

options.text: Chromatography: the salt stays put as the water climbs up
options.rationale: Chromatography compares dissolved substances; it does not recover a solid.

options.text: Crystallisation: evaporate the water until crystals form
options.rationale: The solvent is evaporated and the soluble solid is left behind as crystals.

mcqs.stem: Two liquids are mixed together. Their boiling points are 78 °C and 82 °C. Which method separates them?

options.text: Fractional distillation, because their boiling points are close
options.rationale: A fractionating column is needed to separate miscible liquids with similar boiling points.

options.text: Simple distillation, because only one liquid can evaporate
options.rationale: Both liquids evaporate readily at these temperatures, so a column is needed.

options.text: Crystallisation, because one liquid forms crystals on cooling
options.rationale: Crystallisation recovers a dissolved solid, not one liquid from another.

options.text: Filtration, because one liquid passes through the paper first
options.rationale: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid; both of these are liquids.

mcqs.stem: Black ink is separated by paper chromatography. Which statement about the result is correct?

options.text: The least soluble dye is carried furthest up the paper
options.rationale: The reasoning is reversed: a dye that dissolves poorly is left behind.

options.text: The most soluble dye is carried furthest up the paper
options.rationale: The more soluble a dye is in the solvent, the further the solvent carries it.

options.text: The dye with the smallest particles always travels furthest
options.rationale: Chosen by students who explain the result by particle size rather than solubility.

options.text: Each dye reacts with the solvent to give it a new colour
options.rationale: Chromatography is a physical process; the dyes are unchanged.

mcqs.stem: Rock salt is a mixture of salt and sand. Which sequence gives pure dry salt?

options.text: Filter the rock salt, then crystallise the sand left behind
options.rationale: Dry rock salt cannot be filtered, and the sand is the part to be discarded.

options.text: Dissolve in water, then distil to collect the salt as vapour
options.rationale: Distillation collects the water; the salt does not evaporate.

options.text: Dissolve in water, filter, then crystallise the filtrate
options.rationale: The salt dissolves, the sand is filtered off, and the salt is recovered by crystallisation.

options.text: Heat the rock salt strongly to burn the sand away from it
options.rationale: This assumes a chemical reaction; sand does not burn away and no new substance is wanted.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the physical processes used to separate mixtures is correct?

options.text: New substances are made as the mixture is broken apart
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat any separation as a chemical change.

options.text: A chemical reaction happens, but no energy change occurs
options.rationale: No chemical reaction takes place in filtration, distillation or chromatography.

options.text: The substances are chemically combined by the process used
options.rationale: Combining substances chemically would make a compound, the opposite of separating.

options.text: No new substances are made; the process is a physical one
options.rationale: These processes do not involve chemical reactions and no new substances are made.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about scientific models is correct?

options.text: New experimental evidence may change or replace a model
options.rationale: This is exactly what happened to the model of the atom, repeatedly.

options.text: Once a model is accepted, evidence cannot change it again
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat accepted science as final and proved.

options.text: A model is changed only when scientists agree to vote on it
options.rationale: Models change because of evidence, not because of agreement alone.

options.text: Models are just opinions and are not based on any evidence
options.rationale: Models are explanations built on evidence, not opinions.

mcqs.stem: Before the discovery of the electron, what were atoms thought to be?

options.text: Balls of positive charge with electrons stuck inside them
options.rationale: This is the plum pudding model, which could only come after the electron was found.

options.text: Tiny spheres that could not be divided into smaller bits
options.rationale: This was the model held before the electron was discovered.

options.text: Small spheres each with a charged nucleus at their centre
options.rationale: The nuclear model came much later, from the alpha particle scattering results.

options.text: Tiny spheres orbited by electrons at specific fixed distances
options.rationale: This is Bohr's later adaptation of the nuclear model.

mcqs.stem: What did the plum pudding model suggest about the atom?

options.text: It has a positive nucleus with electrons orbiting around it
options.rationale: This is the nuclear model; the plum pudding model has no nucleus.

options.text: It is a ball of negative charge with positive protons inside
options.rationale: The charges are the wrong way round: the electrons are the 'plums'.

options.text: It is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons in it
options.rationale: This is the specification's description of the plum pudding model.

options.text: It is a ball of neutral matter with no charges inside at all
options.rationale: The model was created to explain where the newly discovered electrons sat.

mcqs.stem: In the alpha particle scattering experiment a few alpha particles were deflected straight back. What did this show?

options.text: Most of the atom is filled with tightly packed positive charge
options.rationale: This is what the plum pudding model predicted, and it was ruled out by the results.

options.text: Electrons must be orbiting the nucleus at particular distances
options.rationale: Bohr's later suggestion; the scattering results said nothing about orbit distances.

options.text: The alpha particles were attracted by the electrons in the atom
options.rationale: Electrons are far too light to deflect an alpha particle backwards.

options.text: The atom's mass and charge are concentrated in a tiny centre
options.rationale: Only a small, dense, charged nucleus could repel an alpha particle backwards.

mcqs.stem: Why did most alpha particles pass straight through the gold foil?

options.text: Most of the atom is empty space, so very few are deflected
options.rationale: The nucleus occupies a tiny fraction of the atom's volume, so most particles miss it.

options.text: Most particles were in fact deflected by the large nucleus
options.rationale: Misremembers the result; deflection was rare and backward scattering rarer still.

options.text: The positive charge is spread thinly, so nothing blocks them
options.rationale: This is the plum pudding explanation, which cannot account for the deflections seen.

options.text: Alpha particles are neutral, so charges cannot deflect them
options.rationale: Alpha particles are positively charged, which is why the nucleus repels them.

mcqs.stem: What is the main difference between the plum pudding model and the nuclear model?

options.text: The nuclear model has positive electrons inside a negative ball
options.rationale: The charges are reversed, and this describes neither model correctly.

options.text: Charge and mass sit in a nucleus, not spread through the atom
options.rationale: The nuclear model concentrates the mass and charge at the centre; the plum pudding model spreads them out.

options.text: The plum pudding model already included a small central nucleus
options.rationale: The plum pudding model has no nucleus at all; that is the change the new evidence forced.

options.text: The nuclear model removed the electrons from the atom entirely
options.rationale: Electrons remain in the nuclear model; they are outside the nucleus.

mcqs.stem: What did Niels Bohr add to the nuclear model?

options.text: The mass of the atom is concentrated in a central nucleus
options.rationale: This came from the alpha particle scattering results, before Bohr's work.

options.text: Neutral particles called neutrons sit inside the nucleus
options.rationale: This was shown by the experimental work of James Chadwick, much later.

options.text: Electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances from it
options.rationale: This is Bohr's adaptation, and his theoretical calculations agreed with observations.

options.text: Electrons are embedded in a ball of positive charge
options.rationale: This is the plum pudding model, which the nuclear model had already replaced.

mcqs.stem: Why was Bohr's adaptation of the nuclear model accepted?

options.text: Scientists accepted it because he was already very famous
options.rationale: Models are accepted on evidence, not reputation.

options.text: It was simpler to draw than the earlier nuclear model was
options.rationale: Ease of drawing is not evidence and played no part in its acceptance.

options.text: He proved his model was true, so it can never be changed
options.rationale: Models are supported by evidence, not proved beyond change.

options.text: His theoretical calculations agreed with the observations
options.rationale: Agreement between calculation and experimental observation is what supported the model.

mcqs.stem: Later experiments showed the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided. What did this establish?

options.text: A nucleus holds a whole number of equally charged protons
options.rationale: Each of the smaller particles carries the same amount of positive charge; they were named protons.

options.text: The nucleus was discovered at the same moment as the proton
options.rationale: The nucleus came first, from scattering; protons were identified by later experiments.

options.text: The nucleus holds neutral particles as well as some protons
options.rationale: Neutrons came later still, from Chadwick's experimental work.

options.text: Each nucleus carries one single, indivisible positive charge
options.rationale: This is the idea the later experiments overturned.

mcqs.stem: What did the experimental work of James Chadwick provide evidence for?

options.text: Protons exist in the nucleus, shown about 20 years later
options.rationale: Protons came from the earlier work on subdividing the nuclear charge.

options.text: Neutrons exist in the nucleus, shown about 20 years later
options.rationale: Chadwick's work came about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted idea.

options.text: The nucleus itself exists, shown about 20 years earlier
options.rationale: The nucleus came from the alpha particle scattering experiment.

options.text: Electrons exist outside the nucleus, shown 20 years later
options.rationale: The electron was discovered before the nucleus, not after.

mcqs.stem: What are the relative electrical charges of a proton, a neutron and an electron?

options.rationale: Gives the neutron a charge and leaves the electron uncharged.
The proton and electron charges have been swapped.
Proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1, as given in the specification.
Confuses the neutron's relative mass of 1 with its relative charge, which is 0.

mcqs.stem: Why does an atom have no overall electrical charge?

options.text: It has the same number of protons as it has neutrons
options.rationale: Neutrons have no charge, and the two numbers are often unequal.

options.text: Its neutrons cancel out the charge on the protons
options.rationale: Neutrons carry no charge, so they cannot cancel anything.

options.text: Its electrons are held well outside the nucleus
options.rationale: Position does not affect charge; the electrons still carry −1 each.

options.text: It has equal numbers of protons and electrons
options.rationale: Each +1 proton is matched by a −1 electron, so the charges cancel.

mcqs.stem: What is the atomic number of an element?

options.text: The number of protons in an atom of the element
options.rationale: Atomic number counts protons, and it is what identifies the element.

options.text: The number of protons and neutrons in the whole atom
options.rationale: This is the mass number, not the atomic number.

options.text: The number of neutrons in an atom of the element
options.rationale: Neutrons vary between isotopes of the same element, so they cannot define it.

options.text: The number of protons, neutrons and electrons in it
options.rationale: Adds every particle in the atom; neither number is defined this way.

mcqs.stem: One atom has 12 protons and another has 13 protons. What follows?

options.text: They are isotopes of one and the same element
options.rationale: Isotopes differ in neutrons; the proton number is fixed for an element.

options.text: They are atoms of two different elements
options.rationale: Atoms of different elements have different numbers of protons.

options.text: They are the same element with different masses
options.rationale: A different proton number means a different element, not a different mass.

options.text: They are two ions of one and the same element
options.rationale: Ions differ in electrons; the number of protons never changes.

mcqs.stem: What is the approximate radius of an atom?

options.rationale: Right prefix, wrong conversion: 1 x 10⁻⁹ m is 1 nm, not 0.1 nm.

options.text: 1 nm (1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m)
options.rationale: The two values do not match: 1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m is 0.1 nm.

options.text: 0.1 nm (1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m)
options.rationale: Atoms are very small, with a radius of about 0.1 nm.
Confuses nano- with milli-; 0.1 mm is about the width of a human hair.

mcqs.stem: An atom has a radius of about 1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m. What is the approximate radius of its nucleus?

options.text: 1 x 10⁻¹¹ m
options.rationale: Assumes the nucleus is about a tenth of the atom, as drawn in diagrams.

options.text: 1 x 10⁻⁹ m
options.rationale: This is larger than the atom itself, so it cannot be the nucleus.

options.text: 1 x 10⁻¹² m
options.rationale: A hundred times smaller than the atom, still far too large for the nucleus.

options.text: 1 x 10⁻¹⁴ m
options.rationale: The nuclear radius is less than 1/10 000 of the atomic radius.

mcqs.stem: An atom's radius is 1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m and its nucleus's radius is 1 x 10⁻¹⁴ m. How many times larger is the atom's radius?

options.rationale: 10⁻¹⁰ ÷ 10⁻¹⁴ = 10⁴, so the atom's radius is ten thousand times larger.
Obtained by subtracting the wrong pair of powers; it also fits the 'nucleus is a tenth' picture.
A common under-estimate from misreading the difference between the two powers of ten.
Off by one power of ten; the difference between −10 and −14 is four, not five.

mcqs.stem: A human hair is about 1 x 10⁻⁴ m wide. Taking an atom's diameter as 2 x 10⁻¹⁰ m, about how many atoms lie side by side across the hair?

options.text: 1 x 10⁶
options.rationale: Uses the atomic radius instead of the diameter, doubling the answer.

options.text: 5 x 10⁵
options.rationale: 1 x 10⁻⁴ ÷ 2 x 10⁻¹⁰ = 5 x 10⁵ atoms.

options.text: 1 x 10⁴
options.rationale: This is the atom-to-nucleus ratio, recalled instead of being calculated.

options.text: 5 x 10³
options.rationale: Comes from a prefix slip that treats the hair as 1 x 10⁻⁶ m wide.

mcqs.stem: How much of an atom's mass is in its nucleus?

options.text: About half of it, since electrons have the same mass
options.rationale: Assumes electrons weigh as much as protons and neutrons.

options.text: None of it, because neutrons have no mass at all
options.rationale: Confuses the neutron's zero charge with zero mass; its relative mass is 1.

options.text: Almost all of it, since protons and neutrons are there
options.rationale: Almost all of the mass of an atom is in the nucleus.

options.text: A tiny part of it, since the nucleus is very small
options.rationale: Size and mass are different: the nucleus is tiny but holds nearly all the mass.

mcqs.stem: What are the relative masses of a proton, a neutron and an electron?

options.text: 1, 1 and 1 exactly
options.rationale: Treats all three particles as having the same mass.

options.text: 1, 0 and very small
options.rationale: Gives the neutron no mass, confusing its zero charge with its mass.

options.text: 1, very small and 1
options.rationale: Swaps the neutron and the electron.

options.text: 1, 1 and very small
options.rationale: Proton 1, neutron 1, electron very small, as given in the specification.

mcqs.stem: An atom has 11 protons, 12 neutrons and 11 electrons. What is its mass number?

options.rationale: Mass number is the sum of the protons and neutrons: 11 + 12 = 23.
This is the atomic number, the number of protons.
Adds the electrons as well; electrons are not counted in the mass number.
This is the number of neutrons only.

mcqs.stem: What is true of two isotopes of the same element?

options.text: Same number of neutrons but a different number of protons
options.rationale: Reverses the definition; a different proton number means a different element.

options.text: Same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
options.rationale: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.

options.text: Same number of protons but different numbers of electrons
options.rationale: This describes ions, not isotopes.

options.text: Different numbers of protons and of neutrons in the nucleus
options.rationale: Atoms of the same element always have the same number of protons.

mcqs.stem: Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are isotopes. How do their atoms differ?

options.text: Chlorine-37 has two more protons than chlorine-35 has
options.rationale: A different number of protons would make it a different element.

options.text: Chlorine-37 has two more electrons than chlorine-35
options.rationale: Extra electrons would make an ion, not an isotope.

options.text: Chlorine-37 has two more neutrons than chlorine-35
options.rationale: Both have 17 protons; the mass numbers differ because of the neutrons.

options.text: Chlorine-37 is a different element from chlorine-35
options.rationale: Both are chlorine because both have 17 protons.

mcqs.stem: An atom is represented as ²³₁₁Na. What do the numbers 23 and 11 show?

options.text: 23 is the atomic number and 11 is the mass number
options.rationale: The two are swapped; the mass number is never the smaller of the two.

options.text: 23 is the number of neutrons and 11 is the protons
options.rationale: 23 counts protons and neutrons together, so there are 12 neutrons.

options.text: 23 is the mass number and 11 is the neutron number
options.rationale: The lower number counts protons; neutrons must be worked out by subtracting.

options.text: 23 is the mass number and 11 is the atomic number
options.rationale: The mass number is written above and the atomic number below.

mcqs.stem: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in an atom of ⁴⁰₁₈Ar?

options.rationale: 18 protons, 40 − 18 = 22 neutrons, and 18 electrons in a neutral atom.
Uses the mass number as the neutron count instead of subtracting.
Reads the two numbers the wrong way round.
Sets the electrons equal to the neutrons rather than to the protons.

mcqs.stem: How many protons and electrons are in the ion ²⁴₁₂Mg²⁺?

options.text: 12 protons and 14 electrons
options.rationale: Adds electrons instead of removing them for a positive ion.

options.text: 12 protons and 10 electrons
options.rationale: The 2+ charge means two electrons have been lost; the protons are unchanged.

options.text: 14 protons and 12 electrons
options.rationale: Changes the number of protons, which would change the element.

options.text: 10 protons and 12 electrons
options.rationale: Removes the protons rather than the electrons.

mcqs.stem: What is the relative atomic mass of an element?

options.text: The mass number of the isotope that is most common
options.rationale: Ignores the other isotopes, and would always give a whole number.

options.text: The plain average of the isotopes' mass numbers
options.rationale: Ignores abundance, so it is only right when isotopes are equally common.

options.text: An average that allows for how common each isotope is
options.rationale: It is an average value that takes account of the abundance of the isotopes.

options.text: The total mass of all the isotopes of that element
options.rationale: It is an average, not a total.

mcqs.stem: Chlorine has isotopes with mass numbers 35 and 37, and a relative atomic mass of 35.5. What does this show?

options.text: The two isotopes are present in equal amounts
options.rationale: Equal abundance would put the average at 36, midway between them.

options.text: Every chlorine atom has a mass of 35.5 units
options.rationale: No atom has that mass; mass numbers are whole numbers.

options.text: Chlorine-37 is much more common than chlorine-35
options.rationale: That would pull the average up towards 37, not down to 35.5.

options.text: Chlorine-35 is much more common than chlorine-37
options.rationale: The average lies close to 35, so the lighter isotope must be far more abundant.

mcqs.stem: How do electrons occupy the energy levels (shells) of an atom?

options.text: They fill the lowest available energy levels first
options.rationale: Electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels, the innermost available shells.

options.text: They fill the outermost energy level first of all
options.rationale: Chosen by students who focus on the outer shell because it controls bonding.

options.text: They spread themselves evenly between the levels
options.rationale: Each level takes a set number of electrons before the next is used.

options.text: They fill the level that matches the group number
options.rationale: The group number tells you the outer electrons, not the filling order.

mcqs.stem: An atom has 17 electrons. What is its electronic structure?

options.rationale: This is 18 electrons; it assumes the outer level must be full.
The first two levels fill with 2 and 8, leaving 7 in the third: 2 + 8 + 7 = 17.
Fills the third level before the second is complete.
Written from the outside inwards, so the levels are in reverse order.

mcqs.stem: Potassium has 19 electrons. What is its electronic structure?

options.rationale: Assumes the third energy level can hold more than eight electrons.
Overfills the second energy level, which holds eight.
After 2 and 8, the third level takes 8 and the last electron starts the fourth.
Starts the fourth level before the third has its eight electrons.

mcqs.stem: Sodium's electronic structure is 2,8,1. What does the 8 represent?

options.text: Eight electrons in the outermost energy level
options.rationale: The outer level of sodium holds the single electron shown by the 1.

options.text: Eight electrons in the lowest energy level of all
options.rationale: The lowest energy level holds the two electrons shown by the first number.

options.text: Eight electrons shared with the third level
options.rationale: Each number belongs to one energy level; electrons are not shared between them.

options.text: Eight electrons in the second energy level
options.rationale: The numbers are read from the innermost level outwards: 2, then 8, then 1.
